We measure whether an LLM finds the gap, with evidence and human review.

lines.text: The rubric author provides a goal, the context, and a draft.
In this case, the incident report must record the start time, the impact on users, and the recovery action. The draft only asks for the probable cause.
When we analyze, only the input goes to the model; the answer key stays with the grader.
This is the real run recorded with qwen2.5:7b on local Ollama, temperature 0, seed 17. A local rerun returned the same six responses, byte for byte.

lines.text: The response follows the JSON contract: status, findings, and a required human decision.
lines.tts: The response follows the jay-son contract: status, findings, and a required human decision.

lines.text: Each finding becomes a card. The evidence is highlighted in the input, and only counts if literal. Then come impact, question, and suggestion.

Here, the model found all three requirements in a single finding. The status is right, and the evidence is literal. Its suggestion splits them into three separate criteria. The content proxy passes this case.
And here is the gate: nothing is applied without human review. The author accepts, edits, or rejects each suggestion.
Even a pass from the lexical proxy is a conservative signal, not a verdict. Semantic equivalence and partial credit need human adjudication.
The dashboard shows the full run: six tasks, one attempt per task, and 24 metagrader tests passing.
lines.tts: The dashboard shows the full run: six tasks, one attempt per task, and twenty-four meta-grader tests passing.

lines.text: Valid protocol on 6 of 6, 100%. Content proxy: 2 of 6, 33%.
lines.tts: Valid protocol on six of six: one hundred percent. Content proxy: two of six, thirty-three percent.

lines.text: Status was right in five of six, but the model never asked for context. Seven of nine answer-key requirements were found. And a second run gave six of six identical responses.
The six cases, quickly. Omissions: all three requirements found, with the right status. The proxy passes.
Insufficient context: it asked what makes a summary useful, but marked the task ready for review instead of asking for context.
Ambiguity: it linked “quickly” to the two business day limit, but only suggested clarifying it, without writing the criterion.
Generic feedback: it ignored the vague feedback in the history and called C1 and C2 ambiguous instead.
lines.tts: Generic feedback: it ignored the vague feedback in the history, and called C 1 and C 2 ambiguous instead.

lines.text: Code: success, explicit error, and continuity are all there. The proxy fails it on word order; the team reads it as a likely false negative.
Iteration: it found the remaining deadline and kept the accepted action. The proxy passes.
In this exploratory run, the hypothesis shows up in part: the model finds explicit omissions, but struggles to ask for missing context, use the history, and make vague criteria verifiable.
Limits: six synthetic tasks, one local model, one attempt per task, and answer keys still pending human adjudication. Next step: frontier models, with three to five attempts per task.
Lacuna. A good grader starts with a good rubric.
